body:
This guide shows you how to convert SVG text to path in Python. You will turn every `<text>` element in an SVG into vector outlines with one save option, look at what the output contains, and process a folder of files.

An SVG `<text>` element stores characters plus a font name. Whoever opens the file needs that font to see the intended lettering. If the font is missing, the viewer substitutes another one and the design changes. Converting text to paths, also called **text vectorization** or "converting to outlines", replaces the characters with the shapes of the letters, so the SVG looks the same everywhere.

## When to Convert SVG Text to Paths

Convert text to paths when the **appearance** of the text matters more than the ability to edit it:

* logos and wordmarks that use a brand font;
* files sent to print shops, cutting machines, or laser engravers;
* SVGs used on websites that don't load the font;
* graphics shared with people whose systems lack the font.

Keep the text as text when it needs to stay editable, translatable, selectable, or searchable.

## Python Library for SVG Text Vectorization

The examples use [Aspose.SVG for Python via .NET](https://products.aspose.com/svg/python-net/). Its `SVGSaveOptions` class has a `vectorize_text` option that performs the conversion when you save. Install the package with pip:

```bash
pip install aspose-svg-net
```

The examples use this `logo.svg`:

```xml
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="400" height="300" viewBox="0 0 400 300">
  <rect x="20" y="20" width="160" height="100" fill="#4A90E2"/>
  <circle cx="290" cy="80" r="55" fill="#F5A623"/>
  <text x="200" y="240" font-family="Arial" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2C3E50">Aspose.SVG</text>
</svg>
```

## Convert SVG Text to Path in Python

Follow these steps to convert SVG text to paths:

1. Load the SVG file into an `SVGDocument`.
2. Create an `SVGSaveOptions` object.
3. Set `vectorize_text` to `True`.
4. Save the document with these options.

The following code example converts the text in `logo.svg` to paths:

```python
import aspose.svg as svg
from aspose.svg.saving import SVGSaveOptions

# Load the SVG that contains text
document = svg.SVGDocument("logo.svg")

# Enable text vectorization
options = SVGSaveOptions()
options.vectorize_text = True

# Save the SVG with text converted to paths
document.save("logo-outlined.svg", options)
```

## What the Output Looks Like

In the saved file, the `<text>` element is gone. Each glyph is stored once as a `<path>` inside `<defs>`, and every letter in the text is drawn with a `<use>` element that references a glyph and positions it with a `transform`. A shortened excerpt:

```xml
<defs>
  <path id="gl_1" d="M-0.052734375,0 l9.896484,-25.769531 l3.6738281,0 ... Z"/>
  ...
</defs>
<use href="#gl_1" transform="..."/>
...
```

Because repeated letters reuse the same glyph definition, the file stays smaller than if each letter had its own full path. In the sample above, the 10 characters of "Aspose.SVG" become 10 `<use>` elements.

The shapes, colors, and positions of the other elements are not changed.

## Convert SVG Text to Path for Many Files

Reuse one `SVGSaveOptions` object to process a whole folder:

```python
import os
import glob
import aspose.svg as svg
from aspose.svg.saving import SVGSaveOptions

input_dir = "svg-files"
output_dir = "svg-outlined"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

options = SVGSaveOptions()
options.vectorize_text = True

for svg_path in glob.glob(os.path.join(input_dir, "*.svg")):
    output_path = os.path.join(output_dir, os.path.basename(svg_path))
    document = svg.SVGDocument(svg_path)
    document.save(output_path, options)
    print("Outlined:", output_path)
```

## Things to Check Before You Vectorize Text 

* **Install the fonts first.** The outlines come from the font the library uses when it loads the SVG. Run the conversion on a machine that has the fonts named in the SVG; otherwise you save the outlines of a fallback font.
* **Keep the original.** Vectorized text can't be edited as text. Store the source SVG alongside the outlined copy.
* **Preserve meaning for accessibility.** Screen readers and search engines can no longer read the words. Add a `<title>` element or an `aria-label` to the SVG if the text carries information.

## Get a Free License

In evaluation mode, Aspose.SVG inserts an evaluation notice into saved SVG files. Request a [free temporary license](https://purchase.aspose.com/temporary-license/) to produce clean output while you evaluate.

## Convert Text to Vector Online

To outline a short piece of text without writing code, try the free [online Text to Vector app](https://products.aspose.app/svg/text-to-vector). Use the Python approach above when you need to process existing SVG files or run the conversion automatically.

## Text to Path: Free Resources

* [Aspose.SVG for Python Documentation](https://docs.aspose.com/svg/python-net/)
* [Aspose.SVG for Python API Reference](https://reference.aspose.com/svg/python-net/)
* [Free Online SVG Apps](https://products.aspose.app/svg/family)
* [Aspose.SVG Blog Posts](https://blog.aspose.com/categories/aspose.svg-product-family/)

## SVG Text to Path: FAQs

**Q: Can I still edit the text after converting it to paths?**

A: No. The letters become shapes. Keep the original SVG if you may need to change the wording.

**Q: Which font is used for the outlines?**

A: The font the library resolves when it loads the SVG. Make sure it is installed on the machine that runs the conversion.

**Q: Is the text still searchable or readable by screen readers?**

A: No. Add a `<title>` or `aria-label` if the meaning must stay accessible.

## Conclusion

You've converted SVG text to path in Python by setting `vectorize_text = True` on `SVGSaveOptions`. The result looks the same on any system, at the cost of editability and searchability, so use it for final artwork rather than working files. If you plan to convert the outlined SVG to PDF or an image next, see [Convert SVG to PDF in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/convert-svg-to-pdf-in-python/).

Questions? Ask on the [Aspose.SVG free support forum](https://forum.aspose.com/c/svg/42).

body:
In this guide, you will learn how to convert SVG to JPG in Python. You will produce a JPEG from an SVG file, get the output to the exact pixel size you want, choose a background color, and then convert a whole folder of SVG files.

[JPG (JPEG)](https://docs.fileformat.com/image/jpeg/) is the format almost every tool, CMS, and email client can display. An [SVG](https://www.aspose.info/page-description-language/svg/) logo or chart often needs a JPG copy for a product listing, a social post, or a document editor that doesn't accept vector files. Since JPG is a raster format, the main decision you make during conversion is **how many pixels** the output should have.

## Python Library to Convert SVG to JPG

The examples use [Aspose.SVG for Python via .NET](https://products.aspose.com/svg/python-net/). It parses and renders the SVG on its own, so no browser or external renderer is required.

Install it from PyPI:

```bash
pip install aspose-svg-net
```

The examples use the following `sample.svg` (400 × 300 pixels):

```xml
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="400" height="300" viewBox="0 0 400 300">
  <rect x="20" y="20" width="160" height="100" fill="#4A90E2" stroke="#1F3B63" stroke-width="4"/>
  <circle cx="290" cy="80" r="55" fill="#F5A623" stroke="#8B5A00" stroke-width="4"/>
  <line x1="20" y1="170" x2="380" y2="170" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="3"/>
  <text x="200" y="240" font-family="Arial" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2C3E50">Aspose.SVG</text>
</svg>
```

## Convert SVG to JPG in Python

Follow these steps to convert an SVG file to JPG:

1. Load the SVG into an `SVGDocument`.
2. Create `ImageSaveOptions` with `ImageFormat.JPEG`.
3. Set `page_setup.sizing` to `SizingType.FIT_CONTENT` so the image is cropped to the drawing.
4. Call `Converter.convert_svg()`.

The following code example converts `sample.svg` to `sample.jpg`:

```python
import aspose.svg as svg
from aspose.svg.converters import Converter
from aspose.svg.saving import ImageSaveOptions
from aspose.svg.rendering import SizingType
from aspose.svg.rendering.image import ImageFormat

# Load the SVG document
document = svg.SVGDocument("sample.svg")

# Configure JPEG output
options = ImageSaveOptions(ImageFormat.JPEG)
options.page_setup.sizing = SizingType.FIT_CONTENT

# Convert SVG to JPG
Converter.convert_svg(document, options, "sample.jpg")
```

The resulting image is **1250 × 938 pixels**, not 400 × 300. The reason is the default resolution of **300 DPI**: the library treats SVG pixels as 1/96 inch and renders them at 300 DPI, so each SVG pixel becomes about 3.1 image pixels. That's handy for print, but probably larger than you need for the web.

Without the `FIT_CONTENT` line, the drawing is placed on a full A4 page (2480 × 3508 pixels at 300 DPI).

## Set the JPG Size and Resolution

To control the pixel size, set the resolution. At **96 DPI**, the JPG has the same pixel size as the SVG. At 192 DPI, it is twice as large in each direction, which is a good choice for high-density screens.

| Resolution | Output size for a 400 × 300 SVG |
|---|---|
| 96 DPI | 400 × 300 px |
| 192 DPI | 800 × 600 px |
| 300 DPI (default) | 1250 × 938 px |

The following code example renders the SVG at 96 DPI. Note that `Resolution.from_dots_per_inch()` expects a float:

```python
import aspose.svg as svg
from aspose.svg.converters import Converter
from aspose.svg.saving import ImageSaveOptions
from aspose.svg.rendering import SizingType
from aspose.svg.rendering.image import ImageFormat
from aspose.svg.drawing import Resolution

document = svg.SVGDocument("sample.svg")

options = ImageSaveOptions(ImageFormat.JPEG)
options.page_setup.sizing = SizingType.FIT_CONTENT
# 96 DPI keeps the SVG's own pixel size
options.horizontal_resolution = Resolution.from_dots_per_inch(96.0)
options.vertical_resolution = Resolution.from_dots_per_inch(96.0)

Converter.convert_svg(document, options, "sample-96dpi.jpg")
```

## Choose a Background Color for the JPG

SVG backgrounds are transparent unless the file draws one. JPG can't store transparency, so transparent areas come out **white** by default. If your brand or page layout needs a different color, set `background_color`:

```python
import aspose.svg as svg
import aspose.pydrawing as drawing
from aspose.svg.converters import Converter
from aspose.svg.saving import ImageSaveOptions
from aspose.svg.rendering import SizingType
from aspose.svg.rendering.image import ImageFormat

document = svg.SVGDocument("sample.svg")

options = ImageSaveOptions(ImageFormat.JPEG)
options.page_setup.sizing = SizingType.FIT_CONTENT
# Light gray background instead of white
options.background_color = drawing.Color.from_argb(255, 240, 240, 240)

Converter.convert_svg(document, options, "sample-gray.jpg")
```

If the image must stay transparent, convert to PNG instead. See [Convert SVG to PNG in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/convert-svg-to-png-in-python/).

## Batch Convert SVG Files to JPG

To convert every SVG in a folder, create the options once and reuse them in a loop. `Converter.convert_svg()` accepts a file path directly:

```python
import os
import glob
from aspose.svg.converters import Converter
from aspose.svg.saving import ImageSaveOptions
from aspose.svg.rendering import SizingType
from aspose.svg.rendering.image import ImageFormat
from aspose.svg.drawing import Resolution

input_dir = "svg-files"
output_dir = "jpg-files"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

options = ImageSaveOptions(ImageFormat.JPEG)
options.page_setup.sizing = SizingType.FIT_CONTENT
options.horizontal_resolution = Resolution.from_dots_per_inch(144.0)
options.vertical_resolution = Resolution.from_dots_per_inch(144.0)

for svg_path in glob.glob(os.path.join(input_dir, "*.svg")):
    name = os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(svg_path))[0]
    jpg_path = os.path.join(output_dir, name + ".jpg")
    Converter.convert_svg(svg_path, options, jpg_path)
    print("Converted:", jpg_path)
```

## Convert SVG to Other Image Formats

The same code works for other raster formats. `ImageFormat` supports `JPEG`, `PNG`, `BMP`, `GIF`, `TIFF`, and `WEBP`. For example, `ImageSaveOptions(ImageFormat.BMP)` produces a BMP file with the same sizing and resolution settings.

## Get a Free License

In evaluation mode, Aspose.SVG adds an evaluation notice to the output. Request a [free temporary license](https://purchase.aspose.com/temporary-license/) to test conversions without this limitation.

## Convert SVG to JPG Online

To convert a few files by hand, use the free [online SVG to JPG converter](https://products.aspose.app/svg/conversion/svg-to-jpg). It runs in your browser and lets you pick a page size before downloading the JPG.

## SVG to JPG: Free Resources

* [Aspose.SVG for Python Documentation](https://docs.aspose.com/svg/python-net/)
* [Aspose.SVG for Python API Reference](https://reference.aspose.com/svg/python-net/)
* [Free Online SVG Apps](https://products.aspose.app/svg/family)
* [Aspose.SVG Blog Posts](https://blog.aspose.com/categories/aspose.svg-product-family/)

## SVG to JPG in Python: FAQs

**Q: Why is my JPG output so large?**

A: The default is 300 DPI on an A4 page. Set `page_setup.sizing` to `SizingType.FIT_CONTENT` and the resolution to 96 DPI to match the SVG's own pixel size.

**Q: What happens to transparent areas of the SVG?**

A: They become white, because JPG doesn't support transparency. Set `background_color` to use another color, or convert to PNG to keep transparency.

**Q: Can I convert SVG to other image formats the same way?**

A: Yes. Pass `ImageFormat.PNG`, `BMP`, `GIF`, `TIFF`, or `WEBP` to `ImageSaveOptions`.

## Conclusion

You now know how to convert SVG to JPG in Python, how DPI determines the size of the JPG, and how to replace the default white background. The key settings to remember are `SizingType.FIT_CONTENT` and the two resolution properties. If you need a print-ready document instead of an image, continue with [Convert SVG to PDF in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/convert-svg-to-pdf-in-python/).

Questions about a specific file? Ask on the [Aspose.SVG free support forum](https://forum.aspose.com/c/svg/42).

## See Also

* [Convert SVG to PNG in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/convert-svg-to-png-in-python/)
* [Convert SVG to PDF in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/convert-svg-to-pdf-in-python/)
* [Convert JPG to SVG in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/convert-jpg-to-svg-in-python/)
* [Convert SVG Code to PNG in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/convert-svg-code-to-png-in-python/)
* [Change SVG Color and Background in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/change-svg-color-and-background-in-python/)
* [Reduce SVG File Size in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/reduce-svg-file-size-in-python/)

paragraphs: In this guide, you will learn how to convert SVG to JPG in Python. You will produce a JPEG from an SVG file, get the output to the exact pixel size you want, choose a background color, and then convert a whole folder of SVG files.

[JPG (JPEG)](https://docs.fileformat.com/image/jpeg/) is the format almost every tool, CMS, and email client can display. An [SVG](https://www.aspose.info/page-description-language/svg/) logo or chart often needs a JPG copy for a product listing, a social post, or a document editor that doesn't accept vector files. Since JPG is a raster format, the main decision you make during conversion is **how many pixels** the output should have.
The examples use [Aspose.SVG for Python via .NET](https://products.aspose.com/svg/python-net/). It parses and renders the SVG on its own, so no browser or external renderer is required.
Install it from PyPI:
The examples use the following `sample.svg` (400 × 300 pixels):
Follow these steps to convert an SVG file to JPG:

1. Load the SVG into an `SVGDocument`.
2. Create `ImageSaveOptions` with `ImageFormat.JPEG`.
3. Set `page_setup.sizing` to `SizingType.FIT_CONTENT` so the image is cropped to the drawing.
4. Call `Converter.convert_svg()`.
The following code example converts `sample.svg` to `sample.jpg`:

The resulting image is **1250 × 938 pixels**, not 400 × 300. The reason is the default resolution of **300 DPI**: the library treats SVG pixels as 1/96 inch and renders them at 300 DPI, so each SVG pixel becomes about 3.1 image pixels. That's handy for print, but probably larger than you need for the web.
Without the `FIT_CONTENT` line, the drawing is placed on a full A4 page (2480 × 3508 pixels at 300 DPI).

To control the pixel size, set the resolution. At **96 DPI**, the JPG has the same pixel size as the SVG. At 192 DPI, it is twice as large in each direction, which is a good choice for high-density screens.

| Resolution | Output size for a 400 × 300 SVG |
|---|---|
| 96 DPI | 400 × 300 px |
| 192 DPI | 800 × 600 px |
| 300 DPI (default) | 1250 × 938 px |
The following code example renders the SVG at 96 DPI. Note that `Resolution.from_dots_per_inch()` expects a float:

SVG backgrounds are transparent unless the file draws one. JPG can't store transparency, so transparent areas come out **white** by default. If your brand or page layout needs a different color, set `background_color`:
If the image must stay transparent, convert to PNG instead. See [Convert SVG to PNG in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/convert-svg-to-png-in-python/).
To convert every SVG in a folder, create the options once and reuse them in a loop. `Converter.convert_svg()` accepts a file path directly:

The same code works for other raster formats. `ImageFormat` supports `JPEG`, `PNG`, `BMP`, `GIF`, `TIFF`, and `WEBP`. For example, `ImageSaveOptions(ImageFormat.BMP)` produces a BMP file with the same sizing and resolution settings.
In evaluation mode, Aspose.SVG adds an evaluation notice to the output. Request a [free temporary license](https://purchase.aspose.com/temporary-license/) to test conversions without this limitation.

To convert a few files by hand, use the free [online SVG to JPG converter](https://products.aspose.app/svg/conversion/svg-to-jpg). It runs in your browser and lets you pick a page size before downloading the JPG.

**Q: Why is my JPG output so large?**
A: The default is 300 DPI on an A4 page. Set `page_setup.sizing` to `SizingType.FIT_CONTENT` and the resolution to 96 DPI to match the SVG's own pixel size.
**Q: What happens to transparent areas of the SVG?**
A: They become white, because JPG doesn't support transparency. Set `background_color` to use another color, or convert to PNG to keep transparency.
**Q: Can I convert SVG to other image formats the same way?**
A: Yes. Pass `ImageFormat.PNG`, `BMP`, `GIF`, `TIFF`, or `WEBP` to `ImageSaveOptions`.

You now know how to convert SVG to JPG in Python, how DPI determines the size of the JPG, and how to replace the default white background. The key settings to remember are `SizingType.FIT_CONTENT` and the two resolution properties. If you need a print-ready document instead of an image, continue with [Convert SVG to PDF in Python](https://blog.aspose.com/svg/convert-svg-to-pdf-in-python/).
Questions about a specific file? Ask on the [Aspose.SVG free support forum](https://forum.aspose.com/c/svg/42).

import aspose.svg as svg
from aspose.svg.converters import Converter
from aspose.svg.saving import ImageSaveOptions
from aspose.svg.rendering import SizingType
from aspose.svg.rendering.image import ImageFormat

# Load the SVG document
document = svg.SVGDocument("sample.svg")

# Configure JPEG output
options = ImageSaveOptions(ImageFormat.JPEG)
options.page_setup.sizing = SizingType.FIT_CONTENT

# Convert SVG to JPG
Converter.convert_svg(document, options, "sample.jpg")

import aspose.svg as svg
from aspose.svg.converters import Converter
from aspose.svg.saving import ImageSaveOptions
from aspose.svg.rendering import SizingType
from aspose.svg.rendering.image import ImageFormat

document = svg.SVGDocument("sample.svg")

import aspose.svg as svg
import aspose.pydrawing as drawing
from aspose.svg.converters import Converter

from aspose.svg.rendering import SizingType
from aspose.svg.rendering.image import ImageFormat

import os
import glob
from aspose.svg.converters import Converter
from aspose.svg.saving import ImageSaveOptions
from aspose.svg.rendering import SizingType
from aspose.svg.rendering.image import ImageFormat
from aspose.svg.drawing import Resolution

input_dir = "svg-files"
output_dir = "jpg-files"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

options = ImageSaveOptions(ImageFormat.JPEG)
options.page_setup.sizing = SizingType.FIT_CONTENT
options.horizontal_resolution = Resolution.from_dots_per_inch(144.0)
options.vertical_resolution = Resolution.from_dots_per_inch(144.0)

for svg_path in glob.glob(os.path.join(input_dir, "*.svg")):
    name = os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(svg_path))[0]
    jpg_path = os.path.join(output_dir, name + ".jpg")
    Converter.convert_svg(svg_path, options, jpg_path)
    print("Converted:", jpg_path)
